Public health officials should consider partnering with external businesses, agencies, and nonprofits to provide public spaces with cleaner air for daytime use. These cleaner air spaces could include senior centers, libraries, and shopping malls. Providing cleaner air spaces during the day can provide an alternative for people unable to reduce smoke levels in their homes, or who are unwilling or unable to evacuate to a designated cleaner air shelter or out of the area to reduce their smoke exposure. Before advertising or advocating for cleaner air spaces, public health officials should confirm that the locations have adequate filtration, ventilation, and cooling/heating capacity to sufficiently condition indoor air based on the expected occupancy. Cleaner air spaces should also have institutional controls to limit smoke infiltration, such as limited door and window use. For more information on improving air quality in non-residential buildings and identifying cleaner air shelters and spaces, see Chapter 3. 5.7 Returning After the Fire Note: This section presents general considerations for dealing with ash and chemicals. It is not intended to replace advice or assessments from professionals or agencies directly involved in cleanup activities. Even after the worst of the fire and smoke is over, individuals who return after the fire should be aware of health and safety hazards. Public health officials should work closely with officials from affected counties to warn residents of health and safety concerns during cleanup and to provide information on best practices for homeowners returning after a fire. This may include creating a list of reputable cleanup or debris removal businesses. 119

Exposure to lingering smoke and ash can cause significant health effects in both healthy individuals and those in at-risk groups. People may experience symptoms including respiratory irritation, heat-related illness, and emotional stress after a fire. Physical stress from cleanup activities, exposure to toxic chemicals, damaged power lines, and equipment such as portable generators can cause injuries during cleanup. Ash from burned structures in the wildland-urban interface (WUI) may contain traces of hazardous substances such as metals (including arsenic, lead, copper, nickel and chromium); asbestos from older buildings; caustic materials; and other chemicals (Plumlee et al. 2007, Villarruel et al. 2024). It is therefore advisable to be cautious and avoid exposure to the ash. In addition, the burned material itself may pose a hazard. For example, products that contain lithium-ion batteries, like electric vehicles, wheelchairs, power tools, game controllers, and other everyday items, can re-ignite, explode, or emit toxic gases if exposed to wildfire. Before beginning cleanup work, it is important to ensure structures are safe to enter, assess the level of cleanup needed, and develop a plan for who will perform the cleanup and how. Professional assistance should be considered if there is structural damage or hazardous materials are present,

to ensure structures are safe to enter, assess the level of cleanup needed, and develop a plan for who will perform the cleanup and how. Professional assistance should be considered if there is structural damage or hazardous materials are present, the HVAC system is impacted, or the scale of cleanup is more than the affected individual can manage on their own. Additionally, smoke often accumulates at the highest level of a home or building. People with attics should consider working with a professional to assess potential impacts to insulation and other materials. FEMA's Homeowner's Guide to Risk Reduction and Remediation of Residential Smoke Damage provides guidance on remediating smoke damage in homes, including tips for selecting a contractor and documenting damage for insurance purposes. Dust masks or filtering facepiece respirators do not protect against asbestos or gases such as carbon monoxide. Avoid handling burned items that may contain hazardous chemicals, such as cleaning products, paint, and solvent containers. Do not touch fire-damaged products with lithium-ion

Avoid handling burned items that may contain hazardous chemicals, such as cleaning products, paint, and solvent containers. Do not touch fire-damaged products with lithium-ion batteries. They should be considered extremely dangerous, even if they look intact. If devices emit popping or hissing noises or are actively smoking or on fire, do not attempt to extinguish or smother the battery. Leave the area immediately, move upwind at least the length of a football field (330 feet) and call 911. Do not start, move, tow or charge a fire-damaged electric/hybrid vehicle or use or start a firedamaged residential energy storage or house battery until it has been assessed and deemed safe by a hazardous material professional. 120

Avoid ash from wooden decks, fences, and retaining walls pressure treated with chromated copper arsenate (CCA) as it may contain lethal amounts of arsenic. Avoid stirring up or sifting through ash if possible; ash deposited on surfaces can become inhaled if it becomes airborne during cleanup. For example, avoid using leaf blowers or dry sweeping. Instead, mist hard surfaces with water before sweeping or mopping. Clean all carpets and soft goods such as couches, mattresses, pillows, pet beds and plush toys using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtered vacuum, if available. Wash homegrown fruits and vegetables. Dispose of ash in the regular trash. If hazardous waste, including asbestos, is suspected to be in the ash, contact local hazardous waste authorities regarding appropriate disposal. Individuals performing cleanup work should wear protective clothing and equipment, such as a well-fitting NIOSH Approved® N95 ® respirator, leather gloves, safety glasses or goggles, long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, and shoes with rugged soles. Individuals temporarily relocating to a new residence during the cleanup of their home should be advised against transporting any ash-covered or smoke-exposed items in their vehicle or to their temporary residence, to reduce exposure. If it is necessary to transport any items contaminated by ash, they should be placed into a plastic bag while wearing gloves and seal the bag completely before placing it in a vehicle. Smoke and ash residue can impact air quality in affected structures. Depending on the severity of smoke intrusion into the building and the duration of exposure, some people may notice visible deposits of smoke and ash residue and/or a lingering odor when they return to their homes, schools, or workplaces. Removing smoke odor is difficult, but there are ways to diminish it, beginning with cleaning and thoroughly airing the structure (Laguerre and Gall, 2024, Li et al., 2023). Every surface of the space exposed to smoke or ash may require cleaning, depending on the extent of the impact. The amount of damage can be assessed with a walk-through of the affected structure checking for visual evidence of smoke and ash residue (e.g., using a white cloth or wipe to check for deposits on surfaces) and smelling for smoke odor. People should be advised to consider seeking professional cleaning or discarding items that are difficult to clean. WUI fires that burn human-made materials can emit chemicals that can be detrimental to health. Chemicals in smoke can deposit on outdoor surfaces and infiltrate into homes. In these cases, consider recommending that household 121

materials such as carpets and upholstery be discarded, especially if there is direct evidence of hazardous contaminants depositing on indoor or outdoor spaces. Cleaning includes wiping down the walls, floors, windows, baseboards, doors, frames, cabinets, furniture, and other surfaces. Cleaning using dry methods, wet methods or a combination of both may be appropriate, depending on the surface. Follow manufacturer's instructions when available. Dry methods, such as vacuuming and using sticky rollers or "soot" or "chem" sponges, generally work well for thick deposits of ash and porous materials. Dry sweeping and dusting are not recommended. When vacuuming, a HEPA vacuum is preferred, if available. If a HEPA vacuum is unavailable, features that make a vacuum more suitable for ash cleanup include true HEPA filters on the exhaust and a sealed system that ensures air passes through the filter. A typical household vacuum or a shop vacuum will send some of the collected dust or ash out into the air. If using these, consider wearing a respirator and using techniques to remove ash and pollutants from the air such as increased ventilation or indoor air filtration. Some people may choose to use additional cleaning products; however, note that some cleaners may also impact indoor air quality. A PAC can be used to remove lingering fine particles (see Chapter 3 for information about selecting and using PACs). Note that while mechanical air filters remove fine particles in the air, they do not remove the gaseous chemicals that cause odors associated with wildfire smoke. These chemicals must be removed by using a PAC with an activated charcoal filter or a filter composed of alumina coated with potassium permanganate. Most portable air cleaner filters for gaseous compounds become saturated quickly and lose effectiveness in smoky environments. They will need to be replaced frequently. PACs with more 122

robust odor removal are available but are frequently expensive. This is why thoroughly cleaning the home interior to remove sources of off-gassing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) is so important. In general, avoid using products that add chemicals to the indoor environment to remove or neutralize smoke odors. The use of an ozone generator to remediate smoke odor is not recommended because ozone can create as many problems as it is intended to fix. Many of the chemicals that are broken up by ozone can produce byproducts that are also dangerous to health. Furthermore, ozone does not remove ash and other particles from the air and indoor surfaces. If an ozone generator is used to remove smoke odors, it should be used only by a remediation professional. The space where the ozone generator is used must be unoccupied during use and for a designated period after use to ensure that no one is exposed to ozone. Some companies claim to use "hydroxyl" generators or other oxidizing technologies such as photocatalytic oxidation (PCO) or chlorine dioxide for remediation. B.1 Introduction When wildfires occur, smoke can impact a wide range of distances, depending on the amount of fire emissions, how high they are lofted into the atmosphere, and the particular meteorological conditions and transport winds. When dealing with wildfire smoke, it is important to consider not only current air quality conditions, such as: * Where is current air quality being impacted? * What have the trends and patterns been over the past several days? but also, to assess fire information: * Where are the fires and how big are they? * How much are they expected to grow? as well as smoke transport downwind: * * * Where are smoke plumes being observed? Where do smoke models say smoke will go over the next few days? Are there diurnal patterns for the smoke impacts? B.2 When Looking at Air Quality Conditions B.2A Considerations Considerations when looking at air quality conditions depend on whether the goal is to determine the current prevailing conditions or to extrapolate recent observed patterns into a prediction for the future, whether the data being used is remotely sensed (e.g. by satellites) or based on ground observations, and what kind of devices are being used to collect the data. Satellite and data fusion products: Satellite based representations of air quality generally show total air column or tropospheric conditions rather than ground concentrations, or ground concentrations are extrapolated based on statistical relationships. Data fusion products incorporate both satellite and ground-based data to create smooth fields of air quality concentrations at the surface. Such products are inherently more accurate close to ground observation locations, in areas away from strong sources of smoke, and in areas with more open terrain. Ground observations using monitors and sensors: Ground-based observations of air quality generally fall into 3 types: (1) established permanent monitoring sites, where siting, maintenance, and quality control are handled by established agencies and owners; (2) rapidly deployed temporary monitoring equipment put out by agencies such as the federal U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality

3 types: (1) established permanent monitoring sites, where siting, maintenance, and quality control are handled by established agencies and owners; (2) rapidly deployed temporary monitoring equipment put out by agencies such as the federal U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality Response Program (see Chapter 1) and state agencies like the California Air Resources Board; and (3) lower cost air quality sensors that may either be owned and deployed by agencies and skilled community groups, but also may be owned and operated by private citizens with unknown training. Each source type has tradeoffs as listed in Table B1. 126

For example, diurnal patterns showing the worst time of day and best time of day are often relatively stable over several days under a consistent weather pattern and fire growth. Trends showing increasing or decreasing impacts of smoke as well as increasing or decreasing

showing the worst time of day and best time of day are often relatively stable over several days under a consistent weather pattern and fire growth. Trends showing increasing or decreasing impacts of smoke as well as increasing or decreasing areas of impact can also be useful. However, to utilize these patterns, additional knowledge is needed. To utilize diurnal trends, knowledge of whether the meteorological patterns are continuing to follow the past several days is needed; if there is a frontal passage moving through that will typically disrupt diurnal patterns. To utilize trends both an understanding of the stability of the meteorological patterns as well as an understanding of how fire growth has progressed and what fire growth is expected to happen moving forward is needed. Trends in air quality conditions are often directly related to trends in fire growth, as fire emissions are, to a substantial extent, directly related to fire growth. 127

B.3 When Accessing Fire Information B.3A Considerations Considerations when accessing fire information include how a recent fire of interest started, how the fire information is being gathered, what the inherent or system-specific delays on that information are likely to be, and what kinds of biases may be inherent to the specific types of information being gathered for display. Generally, fire information falls into 3 types, each with its own characteristics: (1) information from observations and reports by the incident command team (IMT) working the fire (see Chapter 1); (2) information from automated satellite systems that can detect fire hotspots; and (3) information on planned activities by the management team, such as a planned burnout of unburned fuels. Progression of fire information sources: It's often difficult to obtain information about brand new or emerging wildfires and good information from ground reports may take a day or two (or longer) to become available. Until then, the best way to get ground observations about a new wildfire may come as news reports or social media posts as well as automated satellite based remote sensing. Once a wildfire grows to the point that local fire response agencies can no longer manage it, an Incident

about a new wildfire may come as news reports or social media posts as well as automated satellite based remote sensing. Once a wildfire grows to the point that local fire response agencies can no longer manage it, an Incident Management Team will be ordered which will then start feeding information into state and/or national incident response databases. Source type and timing: Information from an IMT and planned activities are generally input by humans and therefore can have greater value due to the data sources' ability to integrate and assimilate information into a coherent narrative. However, the timing of such information usually lags more automated fire tracking from satellites. Reports from IMTs may be up to multiple posts daily to delayed by up to a few days. Reports from IMTs may also include adjusted fire perimeters from ground observations and from aircraft operations. Automated fire hotspot detection is generally available within 1-3 hours of the observation. Fire growth: Satellite hotspots are indicative but not an accurate measure of the amount of fire growth of a fire. Issues with assessing fire growth from hotspots include the pixel size of the imagery of the satellite system which range from approx. 375m to

are indicative but not an accurate measure of the amount of fire growth of a fire. Issues with assessing fire growth from hotspots include the pixel size of the imagery of the satellite system which range from approx. 375m to several kilometers. Satellites typically cannot reliably record whether the fire has consumed all of part of a pixel creating uncertainty in their fire growth estimates. Additionally, the ability of a satellite to observe the fire can be compromised by heavy clouds and/or smoke which sometimes means that satellites will observe no growth (no hotspots detected) during particularly smoky fire growth days. 130

B.4 When Viewing Smoke Plume Extents B.4A Considerations Considerations when viewing a smoke plume extent include how the smoke plume extent was determined and therefore what it represents, the timing of when the smoke plume extent was created, and the relationship of the smoke plume extent with smoke concentrations on the ground. Smoke plume extents are generally derived from satellite observations, from a smoke dispersion model, or from a data fusion product that combines the two. Smoke plume extents are rarely determined from actual observations of ground level air quality as air quality measurements are generally too sparse to generate detailed maps. In some urban areas it is possible to use measurements due to the large number of air quality sensors in the area allowing the creation of detailed progression maps of smoke plumes through the community. satellite fire hot spot detections (NASA WORLDVIEW, September 4, 2017). To learn more, see the NASA Worldview Tutorial by the NASA Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST) at https://haqast.org/nasa-tools. determined from satellites are created by automated algorithms based on various kinds of satellite imagery, by combinations of automated systems and human quality control checking, and, where necessary, human-drawn smoke plumes. A constellation of satellites operates in different Earth orbits, providing different combinations of temporal and spatial coverage. Global observations come from polar orbiting satellites, meaning measurements are collected on 14 pole-to-pole orbits with a field of view of Earth below that shifts ~2600 km each orbit. Depending on the instrument, measurements directly beneath the satellite might be as fine as 30m or more commonly coarser (500m-5000m). The coarser measurements - combined with multiple side-by-side measures - allows for global coverage once per day whereas the finer resolution instruments typically require multiple days or multiple satellites to achieve full coverage. In geostationary orbit, a satellite orbits the Earth at the same rate as Earth rotates, so that the focal area on the ground is consistent. At the focal area (e.g., the continental United States, northern Mexico and Southern Canada),

coverage. In geostationary orbit, a satellite orbits the Earth at the same rate as Earth rotates, so that the focal area on the ground is consistent. At the focal area (e.g., the continental United States, northern Mexico and Southern Canada), the instrument can rapidly repeat measurements at high spatial resolution. The 133

combination of similar instruments in polar- and geostationary-satellites provides global coverage with higher frequency in focal areas and enables cross-platform verification where the two overlap in time and view. Smoke plumes determined by satellites usually represent total air column smoke rather than ground level smoke as satellites generally are most capable of detecting the overall opaqueness of the surfaceto-space air column they are looking through. This can create a good picture of how smoke in one area is connected to the source in another area, because the plume is being tracked no matter what elevation in the atmosphere it travels. It is most easily thought of as tracking where, if you look up, will the sky be orange or hazy as some elevation above you? However, this total air column smoke plume is logically disconnected from what is generally of most concern which is what the smoke concentrations are at the ground. Even "heavy" total air column smoke plumes - representing significant opaqueness of the total air column as detected by the satellite - may not reach the ground or affect air quality to communities. "Heavy" satellite plumes can often be coupled with "GOOD" air quality levels as measured on

representing significant opaqueness of the total air column as detected by the satellite - may not reach the ground or affect air quality to communities. "Heavy" satellite plumes can often be coupled with "GOOD" air quality levels as measured on the ground. Think of an orange sky above but no smell or effects from smoke at the surface. Other considerations for satellite derived smoke plumes include clouds and timing. High clouds can obscure satellite detects of smoke plumes. Clouds are distinguishable from smoke plumes by color (clouds are brighter white) and character and both human and automated systems generally are fairly good at making the distinction. Satellites can only detect smoke plumes during the day as they require reflected light. This means that satellite smoke plumes are not available at night and depending on when the overpasses and/or analyses are scheduled, may not be available until mid-morning. Fog can be another confounding factor which may be marked as smoke on these displays. Smoke plume extents as determined by smoke models or by data fusion products generally try to capture ground level smoke extents. However, some of these products also produce a total air column smoke plume extent to compare to

these displays. Smoke plume extents as determined by smoke models or by data fusion products generally try to capture ground level smoke extents. However, some of these products also produce a total air column smoke plume extent to compare to the satellite smoke plumes as discussed above. Therefore, when viewing smoke model or data fusion smoke plumes it is important to check what variable is being shown. Smoke model and data fusion smoke plumes generally are produced on regularly timed intervals. Satellite observations range from detailed color images that are intuitively valuable to quantitative estimates. Satellites measure light from a variety of sources and different colors. Active satellite instruments measure light that they emit and are less common than passive instruments. Passive satellite instruments measure reflected solar radiation, human lights, or other thermal energy. Anything that relies on direct solar radiation is limited to making measurements during daylight hours. Images of the earth during daylight hours can be reconstructed from measured light of different colors, and are useful for seeing fires, smoke, and plume transport. Analysis of these images is typically qualitative and requires interpretation. For example, the NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons are hand drawn based on these

measured light of different colors, and are useful for seeing fires, smoke, and plume transport. Analysis of these images is typically qualitative and requires interpretation. For example, the NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons are hand drawn based on these images. Satellites can also measure specific colors (spectral bands) which can be used to identify the power emitted from fires or burned areas. Fire power and burned areas are 134

important datasets to estimating air quality emissions from fires. Aerosol optical depth is another measure, which uses reflected solar radiation to measure particulate matter in the atmosphere. Introduction The NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide, PMS 437 (FBFRG) contains helpful references to the factors from the fire triangle (fuels, weather, and topography), including features that are vital to fieldgoing fire managers. It provides detail about fire behavior models and tools used to estimate probability of ignition, spread/size, fireline intensity, and crown fire potential. The reference material is intended to assist with decision support. This guide will be reviewed annually and updated as needed to reflect the most recent science and technologies used to improve and assist with decision support, fireline safety, and fire behavior interpretation. As new and improved safety zone research is obtained and available for distribution, the FBFRG will be updated. Supporting documentation, including instructional videos, will be uploaded periodically to the official YouTube channel: www.youtube.com/user/FireBehaviorSC. Weather Forecast Confidence Forecast confidence is the analyst's professional judgment about how reliable a given fire behavior forecast is based on the quality and consistency of the inputs used to produce it. It communicates to decision-makers how much trust they should place in the prediction, not just what the prediction says. For applications requiring forecast information with very high confidence or accuracy, the typical Confidence Horizon is approximately three

to produce it. It communicates to decision-makers how much trust they should place in the prediction, not just what the prediction says. For applications requiring forecast information with very high confidence or accuracy, the typical Confidence Horizon is approximately three days. However, this horizon is not fixed; shifts in forecast skill routinely expand or contract the period during which very high confidence is achievable, thereby changing the Confidence Horizon. Figure 1. Typical forecast Confidence Horizon. Understanding these shifts is especially important when selecting an appropriate fire behavior modeling tool, applying forecast data within that tool, and documenting assumptions made during analysis. The atmosphere is chaotic, but sometimes there is rhythm in the chaos. Climate outlook scientists study coupled oceanic and atmospheric forcing mechanisms-such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle and Madden Julian Oscillation (MJO)-that influence several teleconnection or long-range, longterm correlated weather patterns that determine meteorological impacts across North America. Forecast skill typically increases (i.e., rhythm in the chaos) for mid- and long-range outlooks when certain forcing mechanisms and teleconnection patterns align. During these periods, the normal NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 1 of 205

Confidence Horizon may extend, allowing monthly or seasonal outlooks to carry medium-to occasionally high-confidence for general weather patterns such as warmer and drier conditions and sometimes frequent wind events. This represents a shift from the typically Low to Very Low confidence associated with longer-range forecasts. Other teleconnection alignments can produce mixed atmospheric forcing signals, thus leading to unusually Low confidence periods (e.g., no rhythm). Best Practices for Determining Weather Confidence Review routinely issued text discussions published by the National Weather Service (NWS), National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) Predictive Services, Storm Prediction Center (SPC), and Climate Prediction Center (CPC). * NWS Area Forecast Discussion - https://www.weather.gov/ This NWS product provides a well-reasoned discussion of the meteorological analysis used to develop the gridded forecast. Forecasters highlight the key challenges influencing the forecast using plain language and wording that reflects their level of confidence. At the end of the discussion section the NWS lists all advisories, non-convective watches, and non-convective warnings. "Non-convective" refers to weather that is not caused by thunderstorms. An intermediate Area Forecast Discussion is issued when significant forecast updates are being made or if interesting weather is expected to occur. * NIFC Predictive Services 7 Day Significant Fire Potential -

Forecast Models Meteorologists produce weather forecasts primarily by interpreting and validating weather prediction models. Several models are available with varying update frequencies, output intervals, temporal ranges, and spatial resolutions. These models are periodically refined as new research, observing techniques, and increased computing capabilities emerge. No singular model is perfect. Forecast models are classified into deterministic, ensemble and convective-allowing models (CAM). Models may be global, regional, or limited to small areas. High resolution models (≤ 5 km) generally fall into the CAM category. CAM operate on smaller areas with 15-minute to 1 hour time-steps and can account for data-intensive convection modeling. They can resolve terrain-induced and altered wind patterns, small-scale boundary passages and banded and cellular precipitation features. Due to the differing scales, physics, and initial conditions, CAMs models can produce widely varying solutions, making it challenging for forecasters to determine which scenario is most likely. Fireline Observations Location and Timing of Fireline Weather Observations There are four key observation times within a 24-hour period that are valuable for assessing forecasts and evaluating thresholds associated with fire behavior transitions: * Early morning observations that capture minimum temperature and maximum humidity. * Late afternoon observations that capture maximum temperature and minimum humidity occur. * Times when active fire behavior increases or diminishes during the burn period. * Hourly observations throughout the afternoon, or whenever conditions change, may be requested by fireline supervisors, or as needed to maintain situational awareness. Selecting an Appropriate Observation Site The weather observer should select observation sites that most accurately represent environmental conditions around the fire. Consider the following: * Determine whether a ridgetop, midslope, or drainage bottom location is most representative. * On slopes, account for aspect and slope steepness. * Identify a fuel bed representative of fire conditions. Do not take observations in nonrepresentative areas such as near bodies of water (with exceptions, as needed), on roads, in the burned area, or next to parked vehicles. * Ideally, choose a safe site upwind or on the flank of the fire. * Saturate the wick of the wet bulb with clean, mineral free water (distilled, if available) at air temperature. * Ventilate thermometers by whirling at full arm's length, arm parallel to the ground, for one minute. * After one minute, read the wet bulb temperature. Calculating Vapor Pressure Deficit Used extensively in greenhouse and agricultural applications, VPD is a strong indicator of green vegetation moisture stress. The Growing Season Index (GSI) incorporates VPD as a key criterion to green-up and curing phenology, with values around 9 mb (millibars) considered optimal for plant growth. While RH expresses the amount of water vapor (moisture) in the air as a percentage of saturation, VPD measures the absolute difference between the actual moisture and the amount it could hold at saturation. Potentially counter-intuitive to RH, VPD increases as the moisture deficit increases and generally follows a seasonal trend, low in winter and higher in warm summer months, driven by variation in temperature and atmospheric humidity. VPD provides important insight about the role of ambient temperature and atmospheric humidity. * At low temperatures, even low RH does not produce a high VPD. * At high temperatures, the same low RH can result in a much higher VPD, indicating a stronger drying potential. Crossover Concept thresholds, where extreme fire behavior exists, are indicated by black boxes on VPD tables. The Crossover Concept The Crossover concept, introduced by the Alberta Forest Service (1985), is a fire weather indicator used to identify potentially critical burning conditions. A "Crossover" occurs when the temperature (in degrees Celsius[C]) exceeds the RH (in %). For example, a temperature of 25°C and a RH of 20% indicates a Crossover situation. Crossover conditions indicate a high potential for fire ignition and rapid spread, especially when combined with wind. The Crossover point is significant because it reflects very dry air and fuels, making it a valuable tool for fire managers in anticipating elevated, dangerous fire behavior. An RH 15% at 60°F has a different effect on the fire environment than at 80°F.

Sky Observations Local terrain and other site-specific factors can modify general atmospheric conditions, creating more localized effects. Weather observers provide important information to meteorologists by reporting the visual cues and the timing of changes throughout the day. Visual cues should be recorded in the remarks section of the weather observation to provide a time-stamped reference. Firefighters should pay attention to both the fire weather forecast and the sky for signs of changing or severe conditions that can influence the fire environment. When visual cues are significant, photographs-paired with a photo log noting location, date, time, and other identifiers-can provide valuable supporting documentation. Airport webcams, available at http://airportwebcams.net/airport-webcams-by-time-zone/, can provide useful real-time information. Synoptic (large-scale) forecasts current-condition reports reference the relative stability of the atmosphere. Several indicators of stability are outlined below. In general, a stable atmosphere suppresses strong vertical motion. Cloud build-ups during stable conditions tend to be broad and flat, sometimes spreading across much of the sky. Additionally, stable conditions favor smoke accumulation near the surface, which can moderate fire behavior due to limited NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 17 of 205

winds, lack of solar radiation to heat fuels, reduced temperatures, and higher relative humidities. However, strong general winds can still occur during stable conditions depending upon the overall weather pattern. In contrast, unstable conditions enhance vertical motion and typically increase ventilation around active fires. Lightning and Wind * Report lightning immediately so fireline supervisors can take appropriate safety precautions and meteorologists can review lightning-detection tools. * Sudden wind shifts may indicate a breaking inversion or frontal passage. The NWCG Fire Weather Cloud Chart, PMS 438, https://www.nwcg.gov/publications/438, provides examples of sky features important for wildland firefighters. Clouds That Indicate Instability in the Atmosphere * Cumulus (various types) - Signal weak instability. They are usually not a concern for firefighters, but continued vertical growth should be monitored. Developing cumulus can precede sudden downdrafts and gusty winds. * Altocumulus (various types, including castellanus) - Indicate increasing moisture and instability in the upper atmosphere and a possible upcoming weather change. Altocumulus castellanus in particular indicate increasing moisture and instability with the potential for thunderstorms. * Cumulonimbus - Reflect very unstable conditions. Fully developed, mature thunderstorms contain extreme vertical motion and can produce sudden gusty, erratic winds-sometimes miles away from the cloud buildup. Severe thunderstorms can generate localized wind gusts over 100 mph along with lightning, virga, hail, shelf clouds or even tornadoes. Clearly, cumulonimbus clouds pose many hazards to the firefighter exposed on the fireline. * Pyrocumulus - Very unstable. The four critical weather elements that may produce extreme fire behavior are low RH, strong surface wind, unstable air, and drought. Critical fire weather patterns that support these conditions can be separated into two primary categories: (1) patterns that produce strong surface winds, and (2) patterns that produce atmospheric instability. In both cases, an unusually dry airmass for the region and season must also occur. In brush and timber fuels, drought becomes an important precursor by increasing fuel availability and receptiveness. Most periods of critical fire weather occur in transition zones between high- and low-pressure systems, at both the surface and upper levels. Surface-pressure patterns of most concern are those associated with cold fronts and terrain-driven foehn winds. Cold front passages are important to firefighters because of strong, shifting winds and unstable air that can enhance the smoke column or produce thunderstorms. Foehn winds occur on the lee side of mountain ranges and are typically very strong, warm, and dry, sometimes abruptly so. The region between the upper ridge and upper trough has the most critical upper-air pattern because of unstable air and strong winds that can mix to the surface. Critical Fire Weather Patterns These descriptions include common terminology used by meteorologists to describe critical fire weather patterns. While you will often encounter these terms in NWS Area Forecast Discussion (AFD), https://forecast.weather.gov/product_sites.php?site=CRH&product=AFD), fire weather planning forecasts, and Predictive Service seven-day outlook assessments, other terminology may be used. East of the Rocky Mountains: Critical fire weather patterns are associated with the periphery of high pressure systems, particularly in the pre-frontal and post-frontal areas. In the Northern Plains, Great Lakes, and the Northeastern U.S., pre-frontal high pressure from the Pacific, Northwestern Canada, and Hudson Bay can produce very dry conditions. Cold fronts can produce relatively short-lived but intense periods of strong winds and instability capable of driving extreme fire behavior. Southeastern U.S.: Drought is frequently associated with La Niña state of the southern oscillation pattern or a blocking ridge aloft near the Atlantic coast. Often critical fire weather patterns follow the frontal passage that brings extremely dry air due to a strong westerly or northwesterly flow. Watch for strong winds that

the southern oscillation pattern or a blocking ridge aloft near the Atlantic coast. Often critical fire weather patterns follow the frontal passage that brings extremely dry air due to a strong westerly or northwesterly flow. Watch for strong winds that accompany the flow. Beware of advancing tropical storms that can produce significant wind shifts as well. Southwestern U.S.: Before monsoons develop, the breakdown of the upper ridge produces breezy, dry, unstable surface conditions that often intensify as the ridge collapses. During transition to the monsoon pattern, shallow monsoons can produce gusty wind, low RH, and lightning without much precipitation. Rocky Mountain and Intermountain Regions: The primary pattern is the upper ridge combined with a surface thermal trough that produces a dry and windy surface cold front. Along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, weather patterns producing Chinook winds bring strong downslope winds that are unusually dry and warm. Across the Intermountain West, critical fire weather is associated with upper troughs, overhead jet streams, or surface-dry cold front passages. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 24 of 205

In the Pacific Northwest, east winds bring strong winds and dry air west of the Cascades. Upper-ridge breakdown is like that described in the Rocky Mountain and Intermountain regions. In California, critical patterns include the north and mono winds in the north and central regions and the Santa Ana and sundowner winds of southern California. The subtropical high aloft brings heat waves. Alaska: Critical fire weather often develops when the upper ridge breaks down and southeast flow brings gusty winds and dry lightning to the interior of Alaska after a period of hot, dry weather. Hawaii: The dry season is May through September, and the wet season is October through April. Critical fire growth events can occur any time of the year when live fuels are drought stricken and/or when herbaceous green-up has senesced. Critical fire weather patterns align with strong trade wind periods when high pressure builds north or when a significant tropical cyclone passes to the south of the main Hawaiian Islands. Hot-Dry-Windy Index The Hot-Dry-Windy Index (HDWI) product suite (https://hdwindex.fs2c.usda.gov/) is designed to help identify days that are more likely to have adverse atmospheric conditions that could make wildland fire management more difficult. HDWI combines surface and low-level atmospheric data into a simple firstlook tool. HDWI is calculated by multiplying the maximum wind speed by the maximum VPD in the lowest approximately 50 millibars of the atmosphere. Because HDWI is affected by heat, moisture, and wind, HDWI values may vary seasonally and regionally when comparing values from different locations and times. Foehn or Downslope Winds Foehn or downslope winds-known by various regional names-occur when stable air is forced over mountain ranges and through mountain passes. These winds are typically warm, dry, and strong. Examples include Santa Ana winds in southern California and Chinook winds along the eastern Rockies. Figure 11. Foehn or downslope wind patterns. Thunderstorm Dynamics: Outflows, and Downbursts Thunderstorms near a fire have the potential to generate outflow gust fronts or downbursts, regardless of whether the storm is influenced by the fire. Any sign of precipitation-rain at the surface or virga aloft-indicates the storm has developed enough to produce these types of winds, along with lightning. Outflow gust fronts spread outward from the base of the storm, usually in the direction of storm motion. They occur with all well-developed convection, can last tens of minutes to an hour or more, and can travel tens to hundreds of kilometers. Downbursts are much less common, shorter lived, and affect a much smaller area but can also produce abrupt changes in wind speed and direction. Either type of wind can abruptly change the speed and direction of fire spread. Figure 12. Thunderstorm dynamics. Sea Breeze Fronts Along coastal regions, sea breeze or sea breeze fronts can bring gusty, shifting winds and changes in humidity and stability that can drive fire behavior. The few hours preceding sea breeze are typically the warmest and driest and coincide with increasing wind speeds and unstable conditions. After the sea breeze front passes, temperatures become cooler while humidity and stability increase.

After the sea breeze front passes, temperatures become cooler while humidity and stability increase. Sea breezes are more critical than land breezes because they occur during the daytime burn period. Tropical Systems Tropical systems, including tropical storms and hurricanes, can create areas of relatively warm, dry, and windy conditions along their northern and western flanks as they move ashore. This may support rapid fire growth. Hot, Dry, and Unstable Events Critical fire growth periods are also tied to hot, dry, and unstable weather patterns. These patterns are typically associated with an upper ridge and a strong mid-level dry intrusion-two ingredients that often precede the breakdown of the upper ridge pattern. A strong "heat bubble," combined with unusual vertical mixing, can produce above normal temperatures (sometimes a heat wave) and very low day and nighttime humidity. The unusual mixing is caused by an unstable atmosphere related to the heat bubble. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 28 of 205

Near the surface, thermal lows may develop and help concentrate this instability. These hot, dry, and unstable weather patterns are normally linked to the subtropical high in the western U.S. and the Bermuda high in the eastern U.S. On rare occasions, the high pressure centers coalesce into a "super high" which can impact large portions of the country. Fire-Slowing or Fire-Stopping Patterns Geographic areas experience fire-slowing and/or fire-stopping periods for three primary reasons: * A partial or widespread change in the weather and fuel regime. * Partial green-up or increased fuel moisture promoted by periods of precipitation. * Temporary changes-such as a cool, moist, stable weather regime replacing hot, dry, and unstable conditions during a multi-day period. Understand that the fire-slowing and/or fire-stopping period is a temporary change. Across the U.S., four main patterns commonly produce fire-slowing or stopping conditions: * Closed low, deep-trough frontal passages * Monsoon bursts * Tropical storms * Smoke events The season-ending period is similar to a fire-slowing period, but the magnitude and duration of change are greater. During a season-ending transition, fuels undergo significant changes-such as long-lasting green-up or a significant rise in larger-sized fuel moisture values. Most regions do not reach season's end

During a season-ending transition, fuels undergo significant changes-such as long-lasting green-up or a significant rise in larger-sized fuel moisture values. Most regions do not reach season's end through a single event; instead, it is a cumulative effect of a series of weather events. For example, the Southwest monsoon evolves over several days to weeks, creating a mosaic of wetting rains and moisture recovery across live and dead fuels. Estimating Winds for Fire Behavior Definitions Critical Winds dominate the fire environment and can easily override local wind influences. Examples include frontal winds, Foehn winds, thunderstorm outflows, whirlwinds, surfacing or low-level jets (reverse wind profiles), and glacier winds. General (Synoptic-Scale) Winds-such as synoptic scale, gradient, free air, and ridgetop-are largescale winds produced by broad pressure gradients between high- and low-pressure systems. They may be influenced and modified considerably in the lower atmosphere by terrain and vegetative structure. Local (Mesoscale) Winds-such as thermal, convective, drainage, and slope winds-develop from local temperature differences generated over comparatively small areas by local terrain and weather. They differ from synoptic winds because they are confined to near surface and are controlled by the strength

Winds-such as thermal, convective, drainage, and slope winds-develop from local temperature differences generated over comparatively small areas by local terrain and weather. They differ from synoptic winds because they are confined to near surface and are controlled by the strength of the daily solar cycle. * Slope Winds are driven by heat exchange at the slope surface. Upslope winds can begin within minutes of solar heating and are influenced by slope length, steepness, and aspect. Typical speeds range from 3 to 8 mph. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 29 of 205

The transition from upslope to downslope wind begins when slopes enter afternoon shadow and cooling of the surface begins. The transition includes: (1) weakening upslope flow, (2) a period of relative calm, and (3) gentle, laminar downslope flow. Downslope winds are very shallow and at a slower speed than upslope winds, generally 2 to 5 mph. The cooled denser air is stable and the downslope flow, therefore, tends to be laminar. * Valley Winds are linked to slope winds but development lags behind slope winds by 1 to 3 hours. Peak speeds can double those of slope winds, reaching 10 to 15 mph. Land and Sea Breeze Circulations form during the day and can reach 10 to 15 mph during peak solar heating in the afternoon. The nighttime land breeze is lighter, generally 5 to 10 mph. According to U.S. weather observing practice, a gust is reported when the peak speed reaches at least 16 knots (18 mph) and the variation in wind speed between peaks and lulls is at least 9 knots (10 mph). Gusts usually last less than 20 seconds. * Midflame Wind Speed is the estimated wind speed at midflame height. This is the wind input used in the Rothermel surface fire model to estimate fire spread. Figure 18. Valley influence on wind strength and alignment. During the day, general winds aligned with up-valley wind will increase surface wind speeds. Opposing winds result in reduced surface winds, while perpendicular general winds have little effect on the local winds. During the night, general winds are most likely to surface when they are strong and aligned parallel to the valley axis. Additional valley considerations are: * Enclosed or Isolated Basins, which typically have reduced surface winds, especially low on the slopes and valley bottoms. Inversions may limit even occasional gusts. * Elongated Valley Winds tend to channel and organize wind flow more effectively than enclosed basins, but they still exhibit distinct day-night patterns driven by terrain-induced circulations. During the daytime, differential heating often promotes up-valley and upslope winds, yet the extent to which general winds surface depends heavily on how well they align with the valley's axis. When the larger-scale flow runs parallel to the valley, general winds can penetrate more readily, producing stronger and more continuous surface winds. Where the alignment is poor, local thermal winds typically dominate, especially in narrower or more sheltered segments. At night, elongated valleys behave more uniformly. Adjusting Surface (20 foot) Wind to Midflame Wind Speed Once general winds have been adjusted to represent 20-foot surface winds based on terrain and other local factors, the next step is to convert 20-foot wind to midflame wind speed (MFWS). MFWS is the velocity of wind at the mid-height of the flames and is always less than the 20-foot wind speed due to the friction of vegetation closer to the surface. This is why adjustment factors are always less than 1. The adjustment depends on canopy sheltering and surface fuel bed depth. The process involves understanding how the wind is oriented with the terrain, whether the terrain is flat or sloped, and a characterization of the canopy characteristics. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 36 of 205

For additional information and examples with student solutions, see the Firefighter Math page about midflame windspeed, found here: https://www.nwcg.gov/course/ffm/fire-behavior/firefighter-math-82midflame-windspeed. Note that the degree of sheltering also varies depending on fire position within terrain features. Adjustment criteria include: For unsheltered fuels, all canopy covers less than 20%, and all crown ratios are less than 0.2. WAF for unsheltered fuel is a function of fuel bed depth only (typically estimated by identifying the fuel model). For sheltered fuels, WAF depends on a combination of canopy cover, canopy height, and average crown ratio for the site. As combinations of these factors increase, WAF transitions from partially sheltered to fully sheltered. Figure 20. Adjusting surface wind for sheltered fuels. TERM Waiting Time Distribution FireFamilyPlus includes a TERM tool (found in the Weather menu) to produce waiting time distributions for historic fire- or season-ending dates. Each year is assigned a single ending date based on established criteria-often developed with input from local fire managers (e.g., a specified amount of rainfall over a defined period). Topography Topography significantly influences fire behavior by altering fuel conditions, wind patterns, and heat transfer. These factors affect fire spread and intensity. Understanding these factors is essential for predicting fire movement and planning effective suppression strategies. Slope Fires spread more rapidly uphill because rising heat preheating fuels ahead of the flaming front. Steeper slopes accelerate this effect, and narrow drainages magnify this effect even more. Fire position on the slope matters; even on a constant slope, fires spread faster at the top of the slope than at the bottom of the slope, a phenomenon known as fire acceleration, making fire behavior prediction on slopes more difficult. A fire starting at the top of a slope cannot readily take advantage of the steepness except when burning debris rolls downhill and ignites fire below. Slope reversals, such as when a fire crosses a drainage and transitions from a backing fire to a head fire, can pose threats to firefighter safety. Strong upslope fires that burn to the top of a ridgeline can roll over the ridge with high intensity, creating lee-side vortices where fire quickly burns back upslope or laterally (Finney et al. 2021). There is much to learn and study regarding

fires that burn to the top of a ridgeline can roll over the ridge with high intensity, creating lee-side vortices where fire quickly burns back upslope or laterally (Finney et al. 2021). There is much to learn and study regarding weather and fire behavior in complex terrain, and fire behavior practitioners are encouraged to study more in publications specifically written for fire managers and fire behavior specialists (Werth et al. 2016, Vol. 1 & 2). Downslope winds often develop as the sun sets as slopes become shaded. These winds are shallow and typically weaker but can become significantly stronger and long-duration when combined over a larger valley extent. Inversions are common in mountainous terrain. As cold air drains into valleys, fire behavior may be suppressed at low elevations while higher terrain remains warmer with lower humidities to support active nighttime fire behavior. Aircraft may be grounded if an inversion significantly affects visibility. When inversions break, a significant increase in fire behavior can occur. Anticipate inversions and adjust fire behavior predictions, strategies, tactics, and safety procedures accordingly. Aspect South- and west-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere receive more sunlight. This can dry the fuels, increasing fire intensity and increasing ignition likelihood.

Aspect South- and west-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere receive more sunlight. This can dry the fuels, increasing fire intensity and increasing ignition likelihood. Conversely, a very dry south aspect may have such sparse fuel that fire does not readily spread, and the more vegetated north aspects may have sufficient fuel to exhibit intense fire behavior. Elevation Lower elevations are generally warmer and drier and may support dry, flashy fuels that promote faster fire spread. Although higher elevations may slow fires due to cooler, moist conditions certain times of the year, they can also support heavier fuel loads that burn with more intensity and have higher resistance to control. The effects of elevation on fire behavior change throughout fire season and vary by latitude. Landforms Landforms, such as canyons, ridges, and valleys, can channel winds, funnel flames, and promote longrange spotting, leading to erratic fire behavior and rapid spread. More complex terrain, with more NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 96 of 205

vertical relief and diverse aspects over a large area, creates significant challenges for fire behavior prediction. Each combination of slope, aspect, fuel type, and wind pattern will result in different fire behavior and presents challenges in predicting fire behavior characteristics. Fuel Moisture Fuel moistures, for both live and dead fuels, can be determined through three primary methods: direct observation, physical sampling, and predictive modeling. Observed fuel moistures involve visual assessment by experienced personnel. These observations provide immediate, qualitative data useful for rapid initial assessments, though they can be subjective and lack precision. Sampling fuel moistures involves collecting fuel materials, weighing them, and drying them to determine their water content. This method provides highly accurate quantitative data but is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and represents only a single point in time that may not reflect conditions across a broader area. Modeled fuel moistures use meteorological data and other environmental factors to estimate moisture levels. These models offer continuous, spatially extensive estimates, which can be particularly valuable for long-term planning and real-time fire management decisions, but their accuracy depends on the quality of input data and the sophistication of the model and may not capture localized anomalies. * VPD: High VPD increases atmospheric demand for moisture, causing water stress. Plants respond by closing stomata (partially or completely), reducing leaf development rate, inducing the shedding of leaves, and slowing or halting cell division. Figure 50. Map of magnetic north across the U.S. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Map Datum Maps use a datum to provide a consistent frame of reference for measuring locations on Earth. A datum defines the size and shape of the Earth (usually as an ellipsoid) and anchors the coordinate system to a specific point, ensuring accurate positioning across different regions and mapping systems. Without a common datum, maps from different sources could show the same location in slightly different places. * Common datums, or Geographic Coordinate Systems (GCS), used in North America include the North American Datum of 1927 (NAD27): a local datum well suited to the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean. Although largely replaced by NAD83, it may still appear in legacy topographic maps, historical land surveys, or older GIS data. * North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83): An Earth-centered datum that corrects NAD27 coordinates based on both Earth and satellite measurements. It is the most regionally accurate datum for North America. This is most likely encountered if using USGS topographic maps. Coordinates are similar to WGS84 coordinates (within 3 to 6 feet) and can be used interchangeably with them. * World Geodetic System of 1984

regionally accurate datum for North America. This is most likely encountered if using USGS topographic maps. Coordinates are similar to WGS84 coordinates (within 3 to 6 feet) and can be used interchangeably with them. * World Geodetic System of 1984 (WGS84): An Earth-centered datum common for datasets with a global extent. Uses the WGS84 spheroid. This is the datum that GPS coordinates are based on and will often be the GCS of files created during helicopter reconnaissance flights. Modern GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS) typically re-projects data "on the fly," but it is important to know why map layers may not be lining up appropriately, especially when using layers from a variety of sources in desktop software applications. Typically, if a shapefile is uploaded as a zipped file, the projection is included, which allows seamless reprojection. Consult a GIS specialist if datasets do not display correctly. Map Projections and Coordinate Systems As noted above, a datum defines Earth's shape and size and the origin point for a coordinate system. A map projection mathematically transforms the 3D surface of the Earth (as defined by the datum) onto a flattened 2D map. Examples are Mercator projection, Albers Equal Area Conic Projection, and Transverse Mercator (UTM) projection. Each will produce a different distortion, either in shape, area, distance, or direction. * LANDFIRE uses the Albers Equal Area Conic projection for national-level data. * WFDSS, IFTDSS, and FlamMap use a custom Albers map projection to preserve area accuracy and provide consistency across the US. For more information on using geospatial data in fire modeling applications, see the Fire Modeling section. A coordinate system defines how locations are measured and expressed on the Earth's surface using the datum (and sometimes the projection). There are two main types: * Geographic Coordinate System (GCS): Uses latitude and longitude based on the WGS84 or NAD83 datum. No projection is applied, so the coordinates are still 3D. * Projected Coordinate System (PCS): Uses planar XY coordinates in meters or feet and usually combines a datum with a map projection. Common PCS examples in fire management

NAD83 datum. No projection is applied, so the coordinates are still 3D. * Projected Coordinate System (PCS): Uses planar XY coordinates in meters or feet and usually combines a datum with a map projection. Common PCS examples in fire management include: * UTM: Divides the Earth into 60 zones that are each six degrees of latitude wide. When using UTMs, note the datum, such as, "NAD83/UTM Zone 12N." The UTM Zone cannot be adequately expressed without also knowing the associated datum. * State Plane Coordinate Systems: Units are projected based on the size and extent of each state. Observing Flame Length vs. Flame Height Flame observations help estimate fireline intensity and indicate tactical limitations. Accurate observation depends on distinguishing flame length from flame height. It is also important to identify whether the observation is from the head, flank, or back of the fire. Flame Length: The distance from the average flame tip to the midpoint of the active flaming zone at the base of the fire. When flames lean due to wind or slope, flame length is measured along the slanted flame angle. Flame Height: The average height of flames as measured vertically is estimated by comparing the flame to a nearby object of known height. Flame height is needed to estimate spotting distance from burning piles. Flame length is commonly used as a proxy for fireline intensity experienced at the actively burning perimeter. Flame height, on the other hand, is what most observers commonly report. Encourage observers to identify which measurement they are reporting and to use the appropriate definitions as described here. Surface Fire NWCG defines surface fire as: "A fire that burns surface litter, debris, and other loose material on the ground. Surface fires may spread by wind, rolling or tumbling of burning material, or by creeping along the ground; they may consume low vegetation and small trees but do not carry fire into the canopy." To estimate surface fire, assume this means within six feet of the ground. The intent of this section is to explain the fundamentals of surface fire predictions and equip personnel with tools and methods for predicting reliable surface fire behavior, enabling timely, informed, safety and tactical decisions on the fireline. When applying the Rothermel spread model, keep in mind that it assumes homogeneous fuels, steady-state conditions, and surface (non-crowning) fire; it does not simulate complex 3-D physics. It incorporates fuel type, moisture content, wind speed, and slope to estimate how quickly a fire will move across the landscape. Predicting Surface Fire Spread Using Lookup Tables Lookup tables provide a quick way to assess potential fire spread and flame length. However, they come with limitations and can only be used for rough estimates. Key considerations when using lookup tables: * Tables only reference the 13 original fuel models (Anderson, 1982). * Tables do not account for spotting or crown fire behavior. * The original 13 models were designed for peak fire season and are not well suited for shoulderseason conditions. * Outputs assume wind is blowing upslope, not across the slope or downslope. When wind is cross-slope or downslope, use a fire spread vectoring process (e.g., Behave), or use the Effective Wind Speed table with an input midflame windspeed (MFWS) of 0 mph for rough estimates. * The original 13 fuel models treat all live fuels (herbaceous and woody) as a single value. In Fire Behavior Fuel Models 2, 4, 5, 7, and 10, a live fuel moisture of 95% is assumed. Grass Fuel Models Fuel Model 1 (Short Grass - 1 foot) Fire spreads through fine, very porous, and continuous herbaceous fuels that are cured or nearly cured. Spread is rapid through cured grass and associated material; very little shrub or timber (less and onethird of the area) is present. Examples include grasslands, savanna, stubble, grass-tundra, and grassshrub combinations. Annual and perennial grasses are included in this fuel model. Fuel Model 3 (Tall Grass - 2.5 feet) Fire produces the highest intensity and highest rates of spread under the influence of wind within the grass group. Wind may drive fire into the upper heights of the grass and across standing water. Stands are tall, averaging about 3 feet (1 meter), but considerable variation may occur. Approximately one-third or more of the stand is considered dead or cured and maintains the fire. Wild or cultivated grains that have not been harvested can be considered like tall prairie and marshland grasses. Figure 58. ROS in Fuel models 1 and 3 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 125 of 205

Grass/Shrub Fuel Models Fuel Model 2 (Timber - Grass and Understory) Fire spread is primarily through fine herbaceous fuels-curing or dead-and through litter and dead/down stem wood from open shrub or timber overstories, which contribute to fire intensity. Open shrublands and pine or scrub-oak stands that cover one-third to two-thirds of the area may generally fit this model. Such stands may include clumps of fuels that generate higher intensities and may produce firebrands. Some pinyon-juniper are included here. Figure 59. ROS in Fuel model 2 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 126 of 205

Brush or Shrub Fuel Models Fuel Model 4 (Chaparral - 6 feet) Intense, fast-spreading fires burn through foliage and live and dead fine, woody material in the crowns of a nearly continuous secondary overstory. Stands of mature shrubs are approximately 6 or more feet tall. Flammable foliage and dead woody material significantly contribute to fire intensity. The height of stands qualifying for this model depends on local conditions. A deep litter layer may also hinder suppression efforts. Examples include California mixed chaparral, the high pocosin along the east coast, the pine barrens of New Jersey, or the closed jack pine stands of the North-Central States. Figure 60. ROS in Fuel Model 4 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 127 of 205

Fuel Model 5 (Brush - 2 feet) Fire carries in surface fuels made up of understory shrub and grass litter or forbs. Intensity is low due to light surface fuel loads-young shrubs, little dead material and limited volatile material in the foliage. Typical of short, green, nearly continuous shrub layers (e.g., laurel, vine maple, alder, or even chaparral, manzanita, or chamise) with no dead wood. Figure 61. ROS in Fuel Model 5 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 128 of 205

Fuel Model 6 (Dormant Brush, Hardwood Slash) Fire carries through the older or dominant shrub layers where foliage is more flammable than Fuel Model 5. Moderate winds (greater than 8 miles per hour, 13 kilometers per hour, at midflame height) are required; fire drops to the ground at low wind speeds or openings in the stand. A broad range of shrub conditions are covered by this model. Examples include intermediate stands of chamise, chaparral, oak brush, low pocosin, Alaskan spruce taiga, and shrub tundra. Even hardwood slash that has cured can be considered. Pinyon-juniper shrublands may be represented but may overpredict ROS except at high winds. Figure 62. ROS in Fuel Model 6 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 129 of 205

Fuel Model 7 (Southern Rough) Fire burns through surface and shrub strata with equal ease. Because live foliage and other live materials are highly flammable, fires can burn at higher dead fuel moistures than in other shrub models. Stands of shrubs typically range from 2 to 6 feet (0.6 to 1.8 m) high. Examples include palmetto-gallberry understory-pine overstory sites, low pocosins, and black spruce-shrub combinations in Alaska. Figure 63. ROS in Fuel Model 7 under different effective windspeeds. Timber Litter Fuel Models Fuel Model 8 (Closed Timber Litter) Fire is generally slow-burning ground fire with low flame lengths, though occasional "jackpots" or heavy fuel concentrations may flare up. Under most conditions the hazard is low, but severe weather conditions involving high temperatures, low humidities, and high winds increase spread potential. Closed-canopy stands of short-needle conifers or hardwoods that have leafed out support fire in the compact litter layer. This layer is mainly needles, leaves, and occasionally twigs because little undergrowth is present in the stand. Representative conifer types are white pine, and lodgepole pine, spruce, fir, and larch. Figure 64. ROS in Fuel Model 8 under different effective windspeeds. Fuel Model 9 (Hardwood Litter) Fire spreads through surface litter faster than Fuel Model 8 and produces longer flame height. This model includes both long-needle conifer stands and hardwood stands, especially oak-hickory types. Fall fires in hardwoods are predictable, but high winds can greatly increase the ROS more than predicted due to spotting caused by rolling and blowing leaves. Concentrations of dead and down woody material can contribute to possible torching of trees, spotting, and crowning. Examples include closed stands of longneedled pine like ponderosa, jeffrey, and red pines or southern pine plantations. Figure 65. ROS in Fuel Model 9 under different effective windspeeds. Timber Understory Fuel Models Fuel Model 10 (Timber - Litter and Understory) Fire burns in surface and ground fuels with greater fire intensity than the other timber litter models. Dead-down fuels- often including greater quantities of 3-inch (7.6-cm) or larger limbs- accumulate on the forest floor due to over maturity or natural events. These heavy fuels increase the likelihood of fire crowning, spotting, and torching, leading to potential fire control difficulties. Any forest type may be considered if heavy down material is present; examples are insect- or disease-ridden stands, windthrown stands, overmature situations with deadfall, and aged light thinning or partial-cut slash. Figure 66. ROS in Fuel Model 10 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 133 of 205

Slash/Blowdown Fuel Models Fuel Model 11 (Light Logging Slash) Fire activity is moderately active, burning in slash mixed with herbaceous vegetation. Fire potential is limited by light fuel loading, shading from overstory trees, or aging of fine fuels. Typical examples include light partial cuts or thinning operations in mixed conifer stands, hardwood stands, and southern pine harvests. Clearcut operations generally produce more slash than represented here. Loads of material less than 3 inches in diameter (7.6 cm) are under 12 tons per acre (5.4 tons per hectare), and fuels greater than 3 inches in diameter (7.6-cm) are represented by no more than ten 4-inch pieces (10.2 cm) along a 50-foot (15 m) transect. Fuel Model 12 (Medium Logging Slash) These fuels can support rapidly spreading, high intensity fire capable of generating firebrands. Once ignited, fire spread is typically sustained until a fuel break or change in fuels is encountered. Slash is the dominant visual feature, consisting mostly of material less than 3 inches (7.6 cm) in diameter. Total fuel load is less than 35 tons per acre (15.6 t/ha) and seems well distributed. Representative conditions include heavily thinned conifer stands, clearcuts, and medium to heavy partial cuts. Materials larger than 3 inches (7.6 cm) are represented by encountering eleven 6-inch pieces (15.2 cm) in diameter along a 50-foot (15 m) transect. Figure 68. Fuel Model 13 (Heavy Logging Slash) Fire is generally carried by a continuous layer of heavy slash. Large quantities of coarse woody material are present. While fine fuels comprise only about 10% of the total load, they carry the initial fires spread quickly, followed by building intensity as large fuels ignite. This model supports active flaming and a wide variety of firebrands, increasing spotting potential. Total fuel load may exceed 200 tons per acre (89.2 t/ha). Stands where the slash still has red needles attached but where total loads are lighter may still be represented, due to high early intensity and quicker area involvement. Figure 69. Spotting and Crown Fire Spotting Spotting fire behavior is a specific situation where embers (firebrands) are lofted from the flaming front and are carried by wind ahead of the main fire front, igniting new fires in receptive fuels. Spot fires can significantly increase the spread and intensity of wildfire. Spotting is typically characterized as shortrange or long-range, though the breakpoint between the two is not universally defined. Additional information about spot fire modeling is available in Behave Help. Short-range Spotting occurs relatively close to the main fire and may not be significant for wildfire growth if the advancing main fire quickly overruns developing spot fires. Spotting distances of a few feet are typically represented in surface fire behavior modeling. Short-range spotting is usually 100 feet to 0.25 miles from the main fire front. Long-range Spotting differs from short-range spotting because firebrands are lofted by a convection column and carried beyond the immediate fire area. Long-range spotting is usually greater than 0.25 miles to several miles. In 2000, the Cerro Grande Fire was reported to have spot fires 10 miles ahead of the fire front. Figure 78. 0.25 miles to several miles. In 2000, the Cerro Grande Fire was reported to have spot fires 10 miles ahead of the fire front. Figure 78. Graphic depicting spotting. Evaluating spotting fire behavior requires three factors: * Source: Size, type, and number of firebrands based on source materials. * Transport: Lofting height and distance the firebrand is carried downwind. * Ignition probability: Likelihood a firebrand will ignite receptive fuels at the landing location. Estimating Maximum Spotting Distance Maximum spotting distance is predicted using equations developed by Frank Albini in the 1970s to estimate how far embers (firebrands) can travel and ignite new fires ahead of the main fire front. It considers: * Firebrand lofting height * Wind speed and direction * Topography (e.g., position on slope relative to wind direction) * Canopy height and tree species Although the maximum spotting distance is calculated, firebrands may land at all the distances up to that maximum. These models are implemented in the SPOT module of Behave, which allows users to input conditions and receive estimates of maximum spotting distance under those conditions. If you're working with Behave, the underlying model for spotting remains based on Albini's work. Figure 80 depicts additional inputs to the Behave spotting module. In mountainous terrain, ridge top winds are used if the wind is blowing across valleys as shown. The shape of the valley is considered with inputs for Ridge-to-Valley distance and elevation difference. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 147 of 205

The maximum spotting distance model requires identification of the tree species, height, and Diameter at Breast Height (DBH) of the torching tree to estimate the flame height and duration from the torching tree that will initiate the lofting of the ember into the wind field. Further, the open windspeed is used to suggest how far the firebrand will be transported as it falls back to the ground. The downwind canopy height, or tree cover, (reduced by half for open canopies) is used to factor embers intercepted by the canopy before reaching surface fuels. Probability of Ignition tables (see Fuel Moisture section) describe only the chance that a landing ember will ignite receptive fuels. Crown Fire Definitions * Crown Fraction Burned (CFB) is a theoretical metric used to model and classify crown fire; it may be observable during post-fire burn severity assessments. It ranges from 0 to 1. * Passive crown fire (intermittent or persistent torching) occurs when surface fire intensity is sufficient to ignite tree crowns (individually or in groups) but winds are insufficient to support sustained crown-to-crown propagation; CFB is typically between 0.10 and 0.90. * Active crown fire occurs when surface and crown fire energies are linked; surface intensity ignites crowns and crown fire spread and intensity reinforce surface fire spread and intensity; CFB is typically greater than or equal to 0.90. * Independent crown fire (rare) occurs when crown fuel loading and flammability alone sustain fire without surface fire contribution under ambient weather and wind conditions; CFB generally approaches 1.0. * Isolated tree torching should not be treated as crown fire, although it may indicate future crown behavior during the burn; it usually results from local anomalies in surface fire behavior, terrain features, or brief wind gusts and corresponds to CFB less than 0.10. Crown Fire Initiation and Propagation In Conditions for the Start and Spread of Crown Fire, Van Wagner (1977), identified crown fire as the interaction between separate fuel layers in forested areas. He described two processes and defined models for estimating their potential. Crown Fire Initiation indicates the potential for a surface fire to ignite tree crowns and produce passive or active crown fire. Inputs include CBH and canopy FMC. The result is the threshold surface fire intensity required to begin canopy combustion. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 156 of 205

Active Crown Fire Propagation (crown spread) indicates the potential for continuous spread through the crown layer. Inputs include a characterization of canopy fuel density (single numeric value). The result is a threshold ROS required to sustain a solid crown flame with associated horizontal spread. These models are coarse because they represent highly variable characteristics (CBH and canopy fuel density) as broad averages; their inputs often require adjustment during modeling. Together, initiation and propagation models estimate when fires will remain on the surface, produce torching or passive crown fire, or progress to active crown fire.
